title: Taste and see (Psalm 33 [34])
hookLine: O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet

cards: Try describing a ripe peach to someone who has never eaten one. Sweet. Soft.
A bit like an apricot. They nod, and still don't know. Then you hand them one, they bite, juice runs down their chin, and now they know, though they couldn't tell you how.
Some things you can only learn with your mouth. When the psalmist wanted to say who God is, he didn't reach for an argument. He reached for a kitchen word.

teach.h: A SONG AFTER A CLOSE CALL.
teach.b: Psalm 33 in the Douay, 34 in most Bibles. Its heading ties it to a low moment in David's life, when he pretended to be mad to escape a foreign king.
Out of that close call comes a song of thanks: "I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth."
In Hebrew it's an acrostic: the verses begin, nearly in order, with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, first to last, a way of saying praise from beginning to end.
Then the line at its center: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet: blessed is the man that hopeth in him." Taste comes before see. First you try it; then you understand.
The psalm isn't asking anyone to agree to an idea about God. It's inviting them to try. Later: "The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a contrite heart: and he will save the humble of spirit."
Near to the broken, not the impressive.
Christians made it a Communion song.

In Jerusalem, in teachings for the newly baptized that tradition credits to Bishop Cyril, the new Christians are told that as they come forward to receive, they will hear a singer chanting, O taste and see.

It's still used as a Communion chant today. This week began with a cry from the cross, walked through the shepherd's valley, lifted city gates, turned on a light, handed a spirit over and broke a long silence.
It ends here, at a table: taste.

how: Catholics hear Psalm 33 [34] at Mass and pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours; its line 'taste and see' has long been sung as a Communion chant and is still used as one.

games.q: someone asks you how to know whether the Lord is good. what does the psalm suggest?
o: wait for a sign in the sky.
games.why: O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet. the psalm invites a trial, not an argument, and early Christians sang it as they came to Communion.

practice: Take one small bite of something nearby, a piece of fruit, a cracker, a sip of tea, or save this for your next meal; don't chew right away, notice the taste arriving, then chew slowly and notice it change.
Don't describe it, just taste. If you pray, give thanks in the psalm's words, taste, and see that the Lord is sweet; if you don't, let the thanks be for the food, and whoever grew it.

wordCard.voice: Acrostic. A psalm whose verses run through the Hebrew alphabet in order, praise from beginning to end. This one invites you to know God the way you know sweetness: by trying it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: taste and see, the psalm's invitation.
